results.text: Why is TCS's volatility so high for such a big company?
results.answer: TCS swings about 31% a year over the last 60 sessions, and the main reason is that this stretch has been unusually jumpy for it, not that it is a risky company. Its price is down 23% this year, yet it rose 22% in the last month, and a fall followed by a sharp rebound pushes the swing figure up. For comparison, the Nifty's own swings are about 11% a year over the same kind of window, so TCS is moving roughly three times as much. Size does not cap volatility: a big company's shares still move on news, results and global tech demand, and Ananta has no study on why TCS in particular swings this much.

results.text: For 3 years, a gold ETF or a gold fund of funds: which and why?
results.answer: For three years, the gold ETF is usually the better pick if you already have a demat account. A gold fund of funds holds the same gold through its fund house's ETF, so you pay its expense ratio on top of the ETF's. The tax rule also favours the ETF: it is long-term after 12 months, while a gold fund of funds needs 24 months, and long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% against your slab rate before that. Choose the fund of funds only if you have no demat account or want small monthly SIPs. Even then, buy gold in small staggered amounts, because GOLDBEES is 21% below its 52-week high (29 Oct) and swings about 18% a year.

results.text: Nifty went up today and open interest also went up. What does that usually mean?
results.answer: Price up with open interest up usually means fresh money is coming in: new long positions are being built, so the rise has some conviction behind it. If open interest had fallen while price rose, it would mostly be shorts closing out, which is weaker. One catch: open interest counts both buyers and sellers, so it doesn't prove who is more aggressive. Treat it as a clue to how strong the move is, not as a signal on its own.

results.text: What happens to a fix after the repair worker builds it?
results.answer: For a safe fix (words, screens, voice, reports, display bugs), the worker runs the test suite right after building it. If the tests pass, it commits the change and puts it live, your phone gets 'Fixed: flag N', and My flags shows 'fixed and live' with the commit. If the checks fail, nothing changes and the flag says so. A fix near trading, a rule, size, stop or cost only gets a written plan, and that waits for your yes.

results.text: Roughly how much margin do I need to sell one Nifty option, versus buying one?
results.answer: Buying one Nifty option needs only the premium, which is the most you can lose. Selling one needs margin, roughly Rs 1-1.5 lakh a lot with the Nifty near 22,700 and a lot of 65 (about 7-10% of a contract worth Rs 14.8 lakh). On expiry day SEBI adds an extra 2% exposure margin on short index options, and a hedged spread needs far less. The exact figure moves daily, so check the broker's margin calculator before you sell.

results.text: What is a long straddle, and in what market does it lose money?
results.answer: A long straddle means buying a call and a put at the same strike and expiry, usually at the money, so you profit if the underlying moves far enough in either direction. You pay both premiums up front, and that total is your maximum loss. It loses money in a quiet, range-bound market, where the price ends near the strike and time decay wears both options down. It also loses if the move is smaller than the combined premium, or if implied volatility falls after you buy, as it often does after an event.

results.text: Does the 87A rebate cover my capital gains?
results.answer: No. From FY 2025-26 the section 87A rebate (the 'no tax up to Rs 12 lakh' of the new regime) does not cover capital gains taxed at special rates, so short-term equity gains (20%) and long-term equity gains (12.5% on the part above Rs 1.25 lakh a year) are still taxed even if your total income is under Rs 12 lakh. These rates apply only if STT was paid, there is no indexation on listed equity, and shares bought before 1 Feb 2018 can use the 31 Jan 2018 price as cost. Surcharge and cess come on top; all of this is as of 27 Oct 2026.

results.text: How is STT charged on options, and what happens if I let an in-the-money stock option expire?
results.answer: Since 1 April 2026, STT on options is 0.15% of the premium when you sell an option (it was 0.10%), and the same 0.15% on the intrinsic value if a bought option is exercised or expires in the money. If you let an in-the-money stock option expire, it goes to physical settlement. The call buyer has to pay the full value of the shares (the seller delivers them), and the contract value also carries 0.1% STT for both sides. Brokers raise margins in the last 4 days and often square off positions that lack the money, so close in-the-money stock options before expiry unless you want delivery.

results.text: My call option lost value after the company's results even though the stock went up. Why?
results.answer: The most likely cause is implied volatility (IV) crush. Before results, option prices carry a big premium for the expected jump; once the numbers are out, that uncertainty vanishes and IV drops sharply, so the option loses value. If the stock rose less than the market had priced in, the fall in IV outweighed your gain from the move. Time decay over the days to results also eats the premium, and an out-of-the-money call needs a much bigger rise just to break even.

results.text: Does ELSS still make sense if I'm on the new tax regime?
results.answer: Mostly no. The new regime gives no section 80C deduction, so ELSS loses its one tax advantage and is just an equity fund locked in for 3 years. If you want that equity exposure, a plain Nifty index fund (Direct plan) gives it without the lock-in. ELSS still makes sense only if you choose the old regime and have unused 80C room. Its gains are taxed like any equity fund, as of 27 Oct 2026: 12.5% on long-term gains above Rs 1.25 lakh a year, only when STT is paid, with no indexation, and the 87A rebate does not cover them.

results.text: Is buying Nifty options on expiry day a good idea?
results.answer: No, as a plain buy-and-hold-for-the-day trade it has not been a good idea. In Ananta's test of Nifty and Bank Nifty options from 2014 to 2023, an at-the-money straddle bought at the open on expiry day lost about 15% of its premium by the close on average after costs (16-19% in 2018-23, which is strong). Time decay is fastest that day, and cheap far-out options are lottery tickets: only 2-3% reach 8x and about 70% of those give most of it back. If you still want to try it, keep it to one small lot you can afford to lose, since SEBI found 91% of individual F&O traders lost money in FY25.

results.text: What tax do I pay if I sell a gold ETF after 14 months?
results.answer: After 14 months a gold ETF is a long-term holding, since the cutoff is 12 months. Your gain is taxed at 12.5% with no indexation, plus surcharge and cess. This is the rule since 1 Apr 2025 (as of 27 Oct 2026). Gold mutual funds and gold fund-of-funds need 24 months for the same treatment, so don't mix the two up.

results.text: What is a calendar spread and why did SEBI change its margin on expiry day?
results.answer: A calendar spread means selling an option that expires soon and buying one on the same underlying and strike that expires later. You gain as the near one loses its time value faster, and the later one caps the loss. SEBI's October 2024 rules removed the margin credit for this pairing on the day the near leg expires (from 1 Feb 2025) and added 2% extra exposure margin on short index options expiring that day (from Nov 2024). The reason is that on expiry day the near option can swing sharply while the far one barely moves, so the "hedge" does not protect against the real risk. SEBI also wanted to curb expiry-day speculation, since it found 91% of individual F&O traders lost money in FY25.

results.text: Should I prepay my home loan or put the money in a SIP?
results.answer: Compare the loan's interest rate with the after-tax return you can realistically expect from the SIP. A home loan at about 8-9% is a certain, risk-free saving when you prepay. Equity SIPs have historically beaten that over 10+ years, but with no guarantee and years of flat or negative returns possible. So first fund the emergency fund (6 months of expenses, 9-12 if income is uncertain), then split: prepay if your rate is above about 9% or the debt makes you uneasy, and favour the SIP if your rate is under about 8% and you have 10+ years. A common middle path is to keep the SIP running and put bonuses or lump sums into prepayment. I'd change this if your loan rate or your time horizon is very different from those assumptions; tell me the rate and how many years you have, and I'll sharpen it.

results.text: How is STT charged on options, and what happens if I let an in-the-money stock option expire?
results.answer: Since 1 April 2026, STT on options is 0.15% of the premium when you sell an option, up from 0.10%. If you let an in-the-money stock option run to expiry, it goes to physical settlement. The buyer of a call must pay for the full value of the shares (a put works the other way round, with the buyer delivering them), and both sides pay 0.1% STT on the full contract value. A bought option that is exercised also pays 0.15% on its intrinsic value. Brokers raise margins from 4 days before expiry and often square off positions that lack the money, so close in-the-money stock options before expiry unless you want delivery.
